title: Montreal Smoked Meat Platter
seoTitle: Montreal Smoked Meat Platter | Firefighter Meal
shortDescription: Steamed brisket-style beef piled high with mustard and rye for ten
subtitle: Steamed brisket-style beef piled high with mustard and rye for ten
description: Beef brisket gets a Montreal-style coriander-and-pepper cure, slow-roasts until fork-tender, then steams and slices paper-thin for a classic smoked meat platter. Serve stacked on rye with yellow mustard, dill pickles, and coleslaw.

steps.title: Gather ingredients and equipment
steps.instruction: Line up every ingredient for Montreal Smoked Meat Platter in the order you will cook — measure spices into ramekins, trim proteins on a dedicated board, and set tongs, thermometers, and hotel pans within arm's reach before any heat goes on.

steps.title: Preheat ovens and surfaces
steps.instruction: Preheat ovens, griddles, or grills to recipe temp before the crew arrives — cold equipment extends cook time and dries out batch beef. Confirm burners ignite evenly and sheet pans are greased or lined.

steps.title: Cure the brisket
steps.instruction: Mix salt, cracked coriander, pepper, garlic powder, and brown sugar. Coat brisket evenly, wrap tight, and refrigerate 24–48 hours, flipping once.

steps.title: Roast low and slow
steps.instruction: Rinse cure lightly, pat dry, and roast uncovered at 275°F fat-side up until probe-tender at 203°F internal, about 4–5 hours. Target oven/smoker temperature: 275°F.

steps.title: Rest and chill slightly
steps.instruction: Wrap brisket in foil and rest 30 minutes. Chill 1 hour if you want cleaner slices—warm meat still works for service night. Keep finished cold items below 41°F if they sit more than 30 minutes — nest the hotel pan on ice at the line. Hold covered at 140°F up to 20 minutes — log the time if your hall tracks food safety during long shifts.

steps.title: Slice and steam
steps.instruction: Slice against the grain as thin as possible. Layer in hotel pans with a splash of warm broth, cover, and steam or hold at 165°F until service.

steps.title: Verify safe internal temps
steps.instruction: Spot-check the thickest pieces with an instant-read thermometer — target 145°F for medium beef, 160°F for ground. If any piece reads low, return it to heat immediately rather than holding under temp on the line.

steps.title: Hold for call interruptions
steps.instruction: If tones drop mid-service, cover finished food and hold at 140°F in a warm cabinet or 200°F oven — never leave proteins below 140°F for more than 30 minutes cumulative. Note the hold time on the pan with a grease pencil.

steps.title: Portion and open the line
steps.instruction: Portion Montreal Smoked Meat Platter onto sheet trays or hotel pans for family-style service. Stack plates, forks, and napkins at the end of the line so late-arriving crew can self-serve without bottlenecking the cook.

steps.title: Scale for larger halls
steps.instruction: When cooking for more than 10 firefighters, split into two pans halfway through so the bottom layer does not overcook while the top waits — duplicate mise en place if you double batches.

steps.title: Build the platter line
steps.instruction: Fan sliced meat on platters with rye, mustard, pickles, and coleslaw. Let crew stack their own sandwiches or plate open-face for speed.

steps.title: Final quality check before service
steps.instruction: Walk the line once before opening service for Montreal Smoked Meat Platter — confirm hotel pans are labeled, backup trays are in the 200°F oven, and thermometers are calibrated. Rookies should ask a senior cook to spot-check the first portion.

proTips: A sharp slicer knife beats a dull chef knife—dedicate one to smoked meat duty.
Save trim for hash or soup base; Montreal-style beef trim is pure flavor.
Offer a side of sauerkraut for crew who want that classic deli counter combo.
tonightSpread: Smoked meat platters with rye, mustard, pickles, and vinegar coleslaw.
Hot fries dusted with Montreal steak spice for a poutine-adjacent side without duplicating poutine night.
leftovers: Chop and griddle with onions for smoked meat hash with fried eggs.
Layer into grilled cheese with Swiss for a hall-style melt.
whyCrewsLikeIt: Smoked meat night feels like a hall field trip to the old neighborhood. Sliced thin and piled high, it feeds fast between tones and satisfies the crew that wants real sandwich meat, not deli turkey from a plastic sleeve.
mealPrepNotes: Cure brisket up to 48 hours ahead for deeper flavor. Steam sliced meat in hotel pans with a splash of broth so it stays moist on the hold line. Slice against the grain as thin as your knife skills allow.
